headline: Women of Uttarakhand safeguard native bee species through ancient tradition
meta_description: In India's Himalayan villages, women maintain traditional wall hives that shelter indigenous honey bees from climate threats and habitat loss.
summary_short: The women of rural Uttarakhand are keeping an ancient beekeeping tradition alive, protecting a vulnerable native bee species through time-honored practices.
body:
In the remote villages of Uttarakhand's Himalayan region, women have become the quiet guardians of an endangered species. They maintain wall hives—rectangular cavities built into the walls of traditional homes—that shelter Apis cerana indica, the Indian honey bee. As modern houses replace traditional ones, these indigenous bees face an existential threat. Between 2001 and 2010, traditional houses in Chamoli district dropped from 61% to 26% of the housing stock, and wall hives plummeted from an average of 11.2 per house to just 0.9. Yet women like Saraswati Devi, 80, and Shakuntala Devi continue a practice so sacred that faag—traditional songs celebrating weddings and festivals—honor the bees' presence. Today, this isn't merely cultural nostalgia: it is conservation work. According to researchers at Kumaun University, women's role as traditional beekeepers is crucial to the species' survival.

The wall hives themselves are engineering marvels suited to the harsh Himalayan climate. Women smooth the interior with clay and cow dung, creating thick mud walls that insulate against freezing temperatures. When outside conditions drop to 10-13°Celsius, the bees remain safely sheltered inside, unable to survive the cold without such protection. In the wild, the same species faces decimation from habitat fragmentation, pesticide exposure, and climate change.

Yet modernization threatens this delicate balance. As rural men migrate to cities for work, women remain as stewards of their ancestral homes—and the bees within them. When families do renovate, new masons often lack the knowledge to build proper hives. One resident, Kanta Devi from Ramni village, discovered this firsthand when her mason constructed a hive too high to maintain. The irony is stark: the moment these homes modernize, they lose their capacity to shelter the very species they've protected for generations. The women of Uttarakhand are racing against time to preserve both a practice and a species.
quick_facts: Indigenous Apis cerana indica bees live in wall hives built into traditional Himalayan homes
Traditional houses in Chamoli district fell from 61% to 26% between 1980 and 2010
Wall hives average dropped from 11.2 to 0.9 per house during the same period
Women maintain hives with clay and cow dung to insulate against mountain cold
Bees survive outside only when temperatures reach 10-13°Celsius (50-55°Fahrenheit)
